24 A vibrating tuning fork is held over a measuring cylinder, as shown.
tuning fork
water
Water is then gradually poured into the measuring cylinder. A much louder sound is first heard
when the water level is 2.9 cm above the base of the measuring cylinder. A second much louder
sound is heard when the water level reaches a height of 67.3 cm above the base.
The speed of sound in air is 330 m s–1.
What is the frequency of the tuning fork?
A
128 Hz
B
256 Hz
C
512 Hz
D
1024 Hz

hints: Notice the two water levels $2.9\text{ cm}$ and $67.3\text{ cm}$ above the base - as water is added the air column above the water gets shorter, so find the change in air-column length.
Recall the air column resonates with a node at the water surface and an antinode near the open top, so successive louder sounds occur when the length changes by $\lambda/2$.
Calculate $67.3 - 2.9 = 64.4\text{ cm}$ for $\lambda/2$, double it to get $\lambda$ in metres, then use $v = f\lambda$ with $v = 330\text{ m s}^{-1}$.
walkthrough: The air column is between the tuning fork at the open top and the water surface below. When water rises from $2.9\text{ cm}$ to $67.3\text{ cm}$ above the base, the air-column length decreases by the same amount.

A louder sound means resonance: a stationary wave forms with a displacement node at the closed water end and an antinode at the open top. Successive resonances differ in length by half a wavelength, $\Delta l = \lambda/2$.
Find the length change: $\Delta l = 67.3\text{ cm} - 2.9\text{ cm} = 64.4\text{ cm} = 0.644\text{ m}$. Set this equal to $\lambda/2$.
Use the wave equation $v = f\lambda$ rearranged to $f = v/\lambda$. Substitute $f = 330/1.288 \approx 256\text{ Hz}$ with unit $\text{Hz}$.

A.explanation: Gives half the correct frequency, equivalent to treating $64.4\text{ cm}$ as a full wavelength instead of half a wavelength.

B.explanation: The $64.4\text{ cm}$ change in water level equals $\lambda/2$, giving $\lambda = 1.288\text{ m}$ and $f = 330/1.288 \approx 256\text{ Hz}$.

C.explanation: Gives twice the correct frequency, equivalent to treating the $64.4\text{ cm}$ separation as one full wavelength $\lambda$.

D.explanation: Gives four times the correct frequency, equivalent to treating the $64.4\text{ cm}$ separation as two wavelengths or misusing the resonance condition.
